title: AI and What It Portends for Young Learners and College Students
author: Michael B. Horn
summary: Horn's general update gathers a week of his own conversations and appearances into a single argument about how schools and colleges should position themselves toward AI. He opens on the New York City and Los Angeles districts implementing different kinds of AI bans and registers his objection: young learners reach AI on home devices anyway, and a blunt ban also blocks narrow, curricularly tailored tools with strong efficacy evidence, naming Amira Learning and Coursemojo. His preferred alternative is neither mandate nor prohibition but exit, the movement of families into publicly funded low-cost private schools and microschools, which he ties to education savings accounts as a vehicle for genuinely disruptive innovation. On the higher education side he argues four years of policies, restrictions, and isolated pilots bought time rather than coherence, and that students are caught in a patchwork of incoherent expectations while the labor market moves faster than the curriculum. Commenting on Jaweed Kaleem's Los Angeles Times piece on new USC and UCLA AI degrees, he sorts current university responses into four curricular developments and flags the real risk that any new program will age badly given slow academic review. Threaded through is his recurring claim that AI makes the experiential and community side of college more valuable, not less, and that entry-level candidates now need real work experience before their first application.
points: Horn's objection to district AI bans is not ideological but practical: bans do not remove home access and do sweep in narrowly scoped tools with efficacy evidence.
He positions microschools and education savings accounts as the third option between forcing AI on families and forbidding it, which lets parents sort by their own circumstances.

His four buckets for university AI curriculum are AI degrees built on a computer science core, AI degrees for non-CS majors, existing degrees that embed AI, and experiential learning that uses AI in the work.
The slow-academic-review problem is his sharpest warning, since a course approved on the usual timeline may be out of date or pointed away from where the field went.
He argues higher education's four years of policies and isolated pilots produced incoherent student expectations rather than a campus-wide strategy that preserves the right level of friction.
quotes: Today’s general update is chock full of pieces about AI: from AI bans in large school districts to college leaders grappling with what the right posture on AI should be—and the implications for learning, career opportunities and more.

Of course, young learners often still get access to AI-enabled tools on home devices. A blunt ban also risks preventing students from getting access to AI-powered applications that are narrow and tailored in their curricular approach—and have strong evidence of efficacy, such as Amira Learning or Coursemojo.

Along those lines, one of my arguments has been that rather than force parents and students into using AI or edtech—or mandating that they avoid it altogether—the increasing movement of families into publicly-funded, low-cost private schools, often of the microschool variety, suggests there’s another way forward.

Higher ed has spent four years managing AI through policies, restrictions, and isolated pilots. That approach bought time, but is time running out? Students are caught in a patchwork of incoherent expectations, and the labor market is shifting faster than the curriculum.

I also drove home the point that shifting expectations, accelerated thanks to AI, in today’s job market means that entry-level candidates need real-world work experience before they apply for their first job.

Horn said the real risk is that any new educational program now will age badly. By the time a course is written and approved through a typically slow academic review, the teaching could be “out of date or in a different direction from the field,” Horn said.
